title: Beautiful but extremely limited
body:
The app is well designed, runs smoothly and is more useful than many other habit developing apps but has a big problem, it is so expensive for what it offers. After the trial ends the free version doesn’t cover the basic needs anymore. And even with the subscription it is very limited on how many habits you can handle. You can only have 6 habits with paid membership and 1 on free version. In my opinion free version should let you manage at least 3 to 5 habits while paid version should not have a limit.
I am still giving this app a 5 stars because it truly deserves it.
author: Fabien Path

title: Preposterous
body:
I am certain that for individuals residing in California or those who can afford to live anywhere globally, a subscription fee of 17 USD per month might seem reasonable for an app. However, in Peru, 69.90 PEN (approximately 18.50 USD) is not just out of touch—it's blatantly preposterous. Considering that 69.90 PEN represents about 6.82% of the minimum wage in a country where over 70% of the workforce is employed informally without insurance, this pricing is excessively unrealistic. I deeply regret this tirade, but I am merely expressing my frustration. Such pricing is illogical outside the wealthiest 1% globally.

A decade ago, the minimum wage in Peru was 750 PEN; today, it is 1025 PEN.

The adjusted subscription fee for Peru, based on purchasing power parity, should be around 16.42 PEN (approximately 4.60 USD) per month. Yet, for every Peruvian outside the wealthiest 1%, 5 USD is still prohibitively expensive for a monthly app subscription. This stark contrast underscores the current pricing's lack of alignment with the local economic reality.

While the app is very well-developed, it mandates the week to start on Sundays (which is not the norm in most countries) and enforces a 12-hour clock format (again, at odds with global standards).
author: Siannath
